The 25x rule:
where it comes from

lines.text: Why does retirement math say you need 25x your spending?
lines.say: Why does retirement math say you need twenty-five times your spending?

lines.text: It's the 4% rule flipped: 1 divided by 0.04 is 25.
lines.say: It's the four percent rule flipped: one divided by point zero four is twenty-five.

lines.text: In 1994, William Bengen tested 30-year retirements back to 1926 and found 4% survived them all.
lines.say: In nineteen ninety-four, William Bengen tested thirty-year retirements back to nineteen twenty-six and found four percent survived them all.

lines.text: A 1998 Trinity study backed it up.
lines.say: A nineteen ninety-eight Trinity study backed it up.

lines.text: Morningstar's forward-looking estimate is lower: 3.9% in December 2025.
lines.say: Morningstar's forward-looking estimate is lower: three point nine percent in December twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Social Security helps: the average check was about $2,071 a month in January 2026, before a 3.6% raise for 2027.
lines.say: Social Security helps: the average check was about two thousand seventy-one dollars a month in January twenty twenty-six, before a three point six percent raise for twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: Our math: $40,000 a year times 25 is $1 million. Subtract about $26,000 of Social Security, and it's $350,000.
lines.say: Our math: forty thousand a year times twenty-five is one million. Subtract about twenty-six thousand of Social Security, and it's three hundred fifty thousand.

lines.text: It's a rule of thumb, not a promise: taxes, fees and bad early years can break it.

post.title: The 25x retirement rule: where the magic number comes from
post.ig:
Why does retirement math say 25x your spending? It's the 4% rule flipped: 1 / 0.04 = 25.
William Bengen's 1994 study tested 30-year US retirements back to 1926; a 4% start survived them all. The 1998 Trinity study backed it up.
Morningstar's forward-looking estimate was 3.9% (Dec 2025). Bengen raised his own figure to 4.7% in his 2025 book.
Our math: $40,000/yr x 25 = $1,000,000. Subtract ~$26,000 of Social Security (avg $2,071/mo in Jan 2026, plus the 3.6% raise for 2027; our math) and it's $350,000.
A rule of thumb, not a guarantee: taxes, fees and bad early years matter.
Sources: Journal of Financial Planning (1994), AAII Journal (1998), Morningstar, SSA.
News and education, not financial advice.
